items.prompt: Let dp(i) be the number of ways to reach step n from i using moves of 1 or 2. Which transition matches that state meaning for i < n?
constraints: Every valid path starts with exactly one move of length 1 or 2.
The two first-move groups are disjoint.

options.text: dp(i) = dp(i) + 1
dp(i) = dp(i + 1) + dp(i + 2)
dp(i) = max(dp(i + 1), dp(i + 2))

feedback.reason: Counting requires summing the disjoint sets of paths created by the two legal first moves.

blocks.text: The state asks for all continuations from i. Every continuation begins with either a one-step or a two-step move, after which the remaining count is dp(i + 1) or dp(i + 2). Because those groups are disjoint and exhaustive, their counts add. Overlap may make this recurrence worth memoizing, but overlap alone does not supply the recurrence or its aggregation operator.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.max_branches: Taking a maximum chooses one branch and discards valid paths from the other branch; the output contract asks for a count.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.self_reference: This does not reduce the unresolved problem and creates a cyclic equation rather than decomposing by a legal move.

items.prompt: For 0/1 selection, dp(i, c) is the best value using items i onward with remaining capacity c. Item i has weight w[i] and value v[i]. Which transition is correct?
constraints: Each item may be used at most once.
Taking item i is legal only when w[i] <= c.

options.text: dp(i, c) = max(dp(i + 1, c), v[i] + dp(i + 1, c - w[i])) when w[i] <= c; otherwise dp(i + 1, c).
dp(i, c) = max(dp(i + 1, c), v[i] + dp(i + 1, c)) for every c.
dp(i, c) = max(dp(i + 1, c), v[i] + dp(i, c - w[i])) when w[i] <= c.

feedback.reason: The take branch must be feasible, consume capacity, and advance past an item that may be used only once.

blocks.text: The skip branch leaves capacity unchanged and moves to i + 1. The take branch is available only when the item fits; it adds v[i], subtracts its weight, and also moves to i + 1 to enforce single use. Every part follows from the state and problem contract. An incomplete index-only state could not express the capacity guard, while a transition that keeps i silently changes the archetype.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_capacity: The take branch neither consumes capacity nor checks feasibility, so it can select overweight items and overstate the optimum.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reuse_item: Keeping i after taking allows the same item to be selected repeatedly; that is an unbounded-choice transition, not 0/1 selection.

items.prompt: A correct recurrence is dp(i) = min(cost[i] + dp(i + 1), cost[i] + dp(i + 2)). What changes when moving from memoization to tabulation?
constraints: Both implementations use the same state meaning and base cases.

options.text: min must become max because bottom-up tables optimize in the opposite direction.
Memoization necessarily evaluates fewer states and is therefore always faster.
The recurrence stays the same; the implementation changes which states are requested or iterated and in what order.

feedback.reason: The recurrence expresses problem structure; memoization and tabulation differ only in how its dependency graph is evaluated.

blocks.text: A state value must be identical regardless of whether it is requested recursively or filled from a loop. Moving bottom-up requires bases and a dependency-safe order, but not a new objective or branch meaning. Top-down can skip unreachable states; bottom-up can avoid call overhead and improve locality. Those trade-offs come after the transition is fixed.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.operator_changes: The aggregation operator follows the objective, not evaluation direction. Changing it changes the problem being solved.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.memo_always_less_work: When every state is reachable, both evaluate the same state set; constants, recursion overhead, and memory locality decide practical cost.

items.prompt: Order the steps for turning a grid-state meaning into a bottom-up transition and schedule.
constraints: dp(r, c) is defined before these steps.
Moves are restricted by the problem statement.

elements.text: List the legal first moves or predecessor choices for (r, c).
Translate each legal choice into the dependent DP state it uses.
Choose the aggregation operator required by the output contract.
Choose row and column directions that make those dependencies available.

feedback.reason: A loop direction is justified only after legal choices have been converted into explicit dependency edges.

blocks.text: Derive the schedule from the transition

items: Enumerate every legal first move or predecessor choice for state (r, c).
Translate each choice into the exact DP state whose value it uses.
Combine those values with the operator required by the output contract: for example sum, min, max or OR.
Choose row and column directions that compute every dependency before the state that reads it.

blocks.text: Starting from the table’s visual layout reverses the reasoning: a convenient loop can read cells whose values are not ready or can implement the wrong predecessor relation. The state meaning and legal moves define the edges; those edges define the schedule.

blocks.title: Transition before loops
blocks.text: Moves → dependent states → aggregation → dependency-safe iteration.

items.prompt: A 0/1 capacity recurrence is compressed to one array. Updating capacities from low to high makes dp[c - w] reflect the current item. What semantic error does this introduce?
constraints: Each item may be used at most once.
Before processing an item, dp represents solutions using only earlier items.

options.text: The result remains correct and only cache locality changes.
The take branch can reuse the current item multiple times because it reads a value already updated in this item layer.
The skip branch becomes impossible, so no item can ever be selected.

feedback.reason: Ascending capacity aliases the previous-item dependency with a current-item value, turning a 0/1 transition into an unbounded one.

blocks.text: The uncompressed take branch reads dp from the previous item layer. In one array, that value is preserved only if capacities are processed descending; then c - w has not yet been updated for the current item. Ascending order lets the current item contribute repeatedly within one layer. Compression therefore requires a revised operational transition whose reads still represent the intended logical states.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.misses_all_items: The previous dp[c] still represents skipping; the defect is repeated use through an overwritten take dependency.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_performance: Update direction changes the logical layer read by the recurrence, so it can change the feasible solution set and the answer.

items.prompt: A maximization DP allows negative values, and an impossible take branch must not be selected. Which representation is safest?
constraints: Valid solutions may have negative total value.
The transition takes a maximum over legal branches.

options.text: Use -infinity or exclude the branch so it cannot win the maximum.
Use 0 so the impossible state behaves like a neutral candidate in the maximum.
Use +infinity so impossible states are distinguishable from finite values.

feedback.reason: An impossible branch must be dominated by every valid maximization result, so -infinity or explicit exclusion preserves semantics.

blocks.text: Sentinel choice is part of the transition contract. In a maximization where legitimate values may be negative, zero is not harmless: it can appear better than every feasible branch. Negative infinity ensures the branch cannot win, while explicit guards avoid creating it at all. For minimization the polarity reverses, and counting usually excludes impossible branches or assigns them zero ways.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.zero: Zero can beat valid negative solutions and fabricate a feasible outcome that the transition never earned.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.positive_infinity: Positive infinity would always win a maximization and make the result invalid.

items.prompt: From each grid cell, moves right and down are legal. Which pair of transitions correctly distinguishes path counting from minimum path cost?
constraints: count(r, c) counts valid paths from the cell.
cost(r, c) is the minimum total cell cost from the cell to the destination.

options.text: Both transitions add successor values because both have two legal moves.
Both transitions take the minimum because a path chooses one next move.
count adds the two successor counts; cost adds the current cell cost to the minimum successor cost.

feedback.reason: The successor states are the same, but counting combines disjoint solution sets by addition while optimization selects the best branch.

blocks.text: Legal moves determine that right and down are the dependencies in both problems. The output contract then supplies the algebra: sum for the cardinality of disjoint path sets, and minimum for choosing one cheapest continuation, with current cost added. Reusing a graph shape does not mean reusing its aggregation operator. This distinction transfers to boolean feasibility using OR and maximum reward using max.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both_sum: The cost contract asks for one cheapest path, not the sum of costs over all paths.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both_min: Counting must include paths beginning with each legal move, so minimizing discards valid path groups.

items.prompt: A 0/1 choice state processes item i with capacity c. Which transition preserves the fact that item i is used at most once?

options.text: max(dp(i + 1, c), value[i] + dp(i + 1, c - weight[i])) when the item fits.
max(dp(i + 1, c), value[i] + dp(i, c - weight[i])) so the same item may be reused.
dp(i + 1, c) because every take branch changes the state meaning.
Add skip and take values because both choices are included in one selected set.

feedback.reason: Both branches advance past item i, so each item is decided once; the take branch additionally reduces capacity.

blocks.text: The skip branch leaves capacity unchanged and moves to i+1. The take branch is legal only when weight[i] fits and then also moves to i+1. Referencing dp(i, ...) in the take branch changes the problem to an unbounded-use recurrence; adding branches would count alternatives rather than maximize one choice.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.take_same_i: Staying at i permits the same item to be selected repeatedly.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.skip_only: The optimum may require taking item i, so omitting that branch changes the feasible set.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sum_branches: For optimization, choose the better alternative; summing counts or combines mutually exclusive choices incorrectly.

items.prompt: Two transitions enumerate the same legal predecessor branches. Which aggregation operator matches a DP that counts all valid constructions?

options.text: Add the predecessor counts, because distinct legal last choices produce disjoint construction sets.
Take the maximum count, because every DP should optimize one branch.
Take the minimum count, because the shortest construction is safest.
Keep the last predecessor visited, because all transitions describe the same path.

feedback.reason: Counting combines disjoint alternatives, while min/max aggregation belongs to different objective contracts.

blocks.text: If a final move can come from two distinct predecessor states, every valid construction belongs to one branch and the sets do not overlap under the recurrence's choice decomposition. Their counts therefore add. Max chooses an optimum, min chooses a minimum, and overwriting loses branches.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.max_counts: Maximization answers a best-value problem, not the number of alternatives.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.min_counts: Minimization also selects one objective value and discards other valid constructions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.overwrite_last: Traversal order is not a semantic aggregation rule and omits earlier branches.

items.prompt: A transition reads dp(i + 1) and dp(i + 2) for a suffix state. What must be defined before using those branches at the end of the input?

options.text: Base meanings for i = n and any branch beyond n, including whether it represents a valid completion or an impossible path.
Let the language return whatever memory follows the table because the recurrence is valid in the middle.
Clamp every out-of-range index to n without checking whether the branch is legal.
Reverse the final answer so invalid end branches cancel out.

feedback.reason: A recurrence is complete only when every referenced state has a declared semantic value at the boundaries.

blocks.text: The end-of-input base may be zero cost, one completion, infinity, or another value depending on the objective. A branch that skips beyond the end may be invalid or may represent a completed construction; the transition cannot decide this implicitly. Memory behavior and clamping are not substitutes for a base-case contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_boundary: Out-of-range access is undefined or wrong even if interior states are correctly derived.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.clamp_indices: Clamping can turn an illegal branch into a valid-looking repeated boundary state.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reverse_answer: A final arithmetic transformation cannot generally repair an incorrectly defined recurrence.

items.prompt: For a DP that chooses or skips an item while maximizing value, what operator usually combines the branches?

options.text: max(skip result, take result) when both branches are legal.
Sum both branches, even though the solution chooses only one.
Take the minimum regardless of the optimization objective.
Use only the take branch for every item.

feedback.reason: The combination operator follows the objective and the mutually exclusive branch choices.

blocks.text: Counting problems may sum branches, minimum-cost problems may take min, and feasibility problems may use OR. Derive the operator from output semantics.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sum_branches: Summing would count two alternatives as if both were selected.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_skip: Skipping can be the optimal legal choice.

items.prompt: Why must a DP transition guard references such as dp[i-1] when i is at the first index?

options.text: The first state may not have that predecessor, so the base case or boundary branch must define its result separately.
Negative indices always refer to the correct empty state automatically.
Boundary checks are unnecessary if the table is large enough.
Sorting indices prevents invalid predecessor reads.

feedback.reason: A recurrence is defined over a valid state domain, and predecessor references must stay inside it or map to an explicit base.

blocks.text: Use a sentinel or initialize base entries before the loop. Do not rely on language-specific out-of-bounds behavior to represent a DP identity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.negative-index-valid: Most languages either reject or give unrelated memory semantics.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.skip-all: A sufficiently large table does not make an index valid.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort-index: Index ordering does not repair an invalid reference.

items.prompt: What changes in a DP transition when the problem asks for counts instead of an optimum?

options.text: Combine legal alternative branches by addition, often modulo the requested modulus.
Always take the maximum branch because DP means optimization.
Keep one arbitrary branch to avoid double counting.
Replace every count with a minimum cost.

feedback.reason: Counts aggregate the number of alternatives; optimization selects one best alternative.

blocks.text: The state and legal branch set may be identical while the combine operator changes. Base cases and modulus behavior must also match the count contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.max-only: Maximum is appropriate only for a maximizing objective.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.min-cost: Cost minimization is a different output semantic.

items.prompt: What is a useful review question when a DP transition seems to use the wrong predecessor?

options.text: What exactly does the destination state mean, and which prior states legally lead to it under that definition?
Whether the loop syntax looks similar to another DP.
Whether allocating a larger table hides the mismatch.
Whether one random input happened to pass.

feedback.reason: Transitions are derived from state semantics, not copied loop patterns.

blocks.text: Write the final decision or last action that produced the state, then enumerate all legal predecessor states. This catches direction and boundary defects before optimization.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.syntax-only: Similar syntax can encode different state meanings.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.table-size: More storage cannot fix an invalid recurrence.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.random-test: One passing example does not prove the transition.
